verses.translation_literal: And it was, when the human [race] began to become many upon the face of the ground, and daughters were born to them,
verses.translation_dramatic: It began in plenty. The human family had started to spread across the face of the ground, village crowding upon village, voice upon voice, and in every house daughters were being born.
verses.directors_commentary: Open wide and warm; this is the last happy sentence before the dark. The text is a plain census report: people multiplying, which Genesis 1:28 had commanded as a blessing. Play it as blessing, so the audience is blindsided by what follows. Note 'ha-adam' (the human, humankind) and 'ha-adamah' (the ground) sound alike; the Hebrew ear hears people and soil in one breath, the same pun as Genesis 2:7. KJV's 'men' narrows 'ha-adam' to males, and it also turns the verb 'began' into a mild 'when men began'; the Hebrew is the hiphil 'hechel', literally 'initiated/began'. Why mention daughters at all? Radak says births of both sexes are a given, so the mention sets up the daughters as the occasion of what comes next. Ancient audiences also lived in a world of high infant loss and small settlements; a growing population was wealth, labour and security, not yet a problem.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of chalal, 'to begin'. A different root from chalal 'to pierce/profane'; Ibn Ezra notes it is from the 'hiphil' pattern meaning 'started'. Sets a beginning for the spiral that follows.
'The human(kind)', with the article, not 'men' as KJV. Plays on 'ha-adamah', the ground, in the same verse.

verses.translation_literal: And the sons of the God saw the daughters of the human that good [were] they, and they took for themselves women from all whom they chose.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the sons of God looked, and what they saw was the daughters of men: how good they were to see. They looked, and they wanted, and they reached out. They took wives for themselves, whoever they chose, from all who were there.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs carry the scene: saw, took, chose. It is the chain of Genesis 3:6, where the woman 'saw that the tree was good... and took'. Play the seeing as appetite, not admiration. 'Good' (tov) is the word God spoke over creation; here it is a judgment made by the one who takes. KJV's 'fair' narrows it to looks; the Hebrew says 'good'. KJV's 'wives' is also gentler than 'nashim', the ordinary word for 'women', and 'took' is the verb for taking by right or by force.

Who are the sons of God? The old readers split, and the director should not pick for the audience. Onkelos and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on this verse both say 'sons of the great' (bene rabrevaya), and Rashi, Ramban and Radak hear judges and nobles, men whose rank let them take and whom no one could refuse. Rashi also gives a second reading: the princes, or the angels, who go on the Place's errand and mingled with humans. The angelic reading is spelled out in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on 6:4, which names Shamhazai and Uzziel as beings who fell from heaven. Ibn Ezra reports that 'some say' they are the sons of Seth and the daughters of men the line of Cain; his own preference is that they were those who knew the Most High and chose wives by the stars. Ramban stresses that the sin is violence in the taking: 'from all whom they chose' leaves no woman free to refuse. Elsewhere 'sons of God' can name God's heavenly court (Job 1:6); that is my own context, not a source claim.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'sons of the God/gods'. 'Elohim' is plural in form and can mean God, gods or rulers. Identity disputed: judges, nobles and princes (Rashi, Ramban, Radak; Onkelos and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan here have 'sons of the great'); princes or angels on the Place's errand (Rashi's second reading); the line of Seth, reported by Ibn Ezra as 'some say', while he prefers those who knew the Most High. The angelic reading is Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on 6:4, not on 6:2.
'Good', feminine plural. Rashi cites R. Judan: the spelling can be read as 'made good', i.e. adorned before the wedding. KJV 'fair' narrows the sense.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH said, "Not shall abide my spirit in the human for ever, in that also he [is] flesh; and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years."
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD spoke. "My spirit will not stay in humankind forever. They are flesh, only flesh. Their days shall be a hundred and twenty years."
verses.directors_commentary: A quiet verdict, not a shout. The weight sits on two words: 'ruchi' (my spirit, breath) and 'basar' (flesh). The breath God breathed into the first human (2:7) is not to be left in them without limit. The verb 'yadon' is a famous puzzle: no certain meaning. Rashi and Radak connect it to 'contend, strive' (as in 'madon', quarrel), Ibn Ezra to a 'sheath' for the spirit; the Targums have 'be established'. KJV's 'strive with' picks one; the Hebrew leaves it open. 'Beshagam' is also odd: most read it as 'since also', 'because moreover'. The 120 years: Rashi, Radak, Sforno and Onkelos read it as a period of grace to repent (Noah building and warning, Sforno), not as the new human lifespan, which later chapters contradict (Ibn Ezra). Rashi notes that Shem, Ham and Japheth were not yet born 120 years before the flood, so the decree came earlier than its telling. A reader should hear mercy built into a sentence: a countdown that is also a delay.

philological_notes.note: Meaning uncertain. Options: 'contend/strive' (Rashi, Radak, from din/madon), 'abide' as a spirit within a body-sheath (Ibn Ezra, Radak citing nadan), 'be judged'. The Targums render 'be established'. KJV 'strive' follows the first.
A single word that reads as be-she-gam, 'in that also / because also'. Rashi and Radak parallel it with 'shaqqamti Devorah' (Judges 5:7) where she- stands for asher.
'Flesh': human frailty and mortality, set against God's spirit. Not necessarily sinfulness; Ramban hears the contrast with spirit, Sforno that flesh invites mercy.

verses.translation_literal: The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when the sons of the God would go in to the daughters of the human, and they bore [children] to them; they [were] the mighty ones who [were] from of old, the men of the name.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Nephilim walked the earth in those days, and in the days after, whenever the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore children to them. These were the heroes, the ones of old: the men of the name.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the strangest verse in the story, so do not play it as certain. 'Nephilim' stays untranslated in the dramatic layer. The root nafal means 'fall', and the etymology 'fallen ones' stands: Rashi says they fell and made the world fall. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it differently: the sight of them makes the onlooker's heart fall, in awe at their height.

The verse itself states no size. But Rashi ('anakim'), Ibn Ezra (their stature) and Radak ('very tall') all understand the Nephilim as giants, so KJV's 'giants' follows an old reading and is not an addition. Anyone who hears 'Anakim' will recall Numbers 13:33, where the spies call the people of Canaan Nephilim; that link is my own observation. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names two beings fallen from heaven, Shamhazai and Uzziel.

The verb 'yavo'u' ('would go in') is habitual, 'again and again', and 'go in to' is the Hebrew euphemism for sex; KJV's 'came in unto' keeps it. 'Anshe ha-shem', 'men of the name', means famous men, and a Hebrew ear may hear the 'shem' that the builders of Babel crave in 11:4 (my own observation). Rashi hears the pun the other way: shem as desolation (shamam), men who laid the world waste. 'Hemmah' (they) points back: these are the heroes of the legends your audience already knows.

philological_notes.note: From nafal 'to fall'. 'Fallen ones' is the etymology (Rashi: they fell and made the world fall); Ibn Ezra and Radak: those whose sight makes the heart of the onlooker fall. The verse gives no size, but Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak understand giants, so KJV 'giants' follows an old reading. The Numbers 13:33 link is my own observation.
'Men of the name', famous men (Radak: they had a name in the mouths of later generations). Rashi also hears 'men of desolation' (shamam), those who laid the world waste.
Imperfect form, 'would go in', habitual. 'Go in to' is the euphemism for intercourse.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH saw that great [was] the evil of the human in the earth, and every formation of the thoughts of his heart [was] only evil all the day.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD saw it: how great the evil of man had grown on the earth, and that every shape the heart gave its thinking was only evil, the whole day long.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the narrator lets God look. The verb 'saw' is the one used for each day of creation ('and God saw that it was good'); now the seeing finds the reverse. The sentence builds in a stack: evil great, then every 'yetzer' (what is formed or moulded) of the thoughts of the heart, then 'only evil', then 'all the day'. 'Yetzer' comes from the potter's verb 'yatzar' (as in 2:7, where God formed the human); the heart now moulds something other than what its Maker intended. KJV's 'imagination of the thoughts' is accurate but archaic; the Hebrew says 'the formation of the plans of the heart'. 'Continually' is KJV's reading of 'kol ha-yom', literally 'all the day', which gives the sense of a day that never lets up. Radak says it means the inclination was entirely evil, with no good left. Sforno separates the two halves: the first clause looks back (what they had done), the second forward (they would not listen to a rebuke). Mind the heart: in Hebrew psychology the 'lev' is the seat of thought and will, not feeling alone.

philological_notes.note: From yatzar 'to form, mould' (a potter's word). The shaped product of the heart, its inclination or design. Radak links it to the heart forming matters for good or evil.
Literally 'all the day', all day long, continually. Radak sees it as worsening each day.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH regretted that he had made the human in the earth, and he was pained to his heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD was sorry that he had made man on the earth. Grief took him, and it closed around his heart.
verses.directors_commentary: Do not play anger. The text gives grief. Two verbs: 'vayinnachem' (he regretted, was sorry, changed his mind) and 'vayit'atstsev' (he was pained, grieved). The second shares its root with 'etsev', the pain of childbirth and toil God pronounced in 3:16-17: God now feels what he told humanity it would feel. KJV's 'it repented the Lord' is archaic and invites the wrong reading, a God who sinned; the verb is about a change of heart, and the same root, 'nacham', also gives 'comfort'. The great medieval commentators are uneasy: Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban all say 'the Torah speaks in human language' and that God does not literally change. Rashi stresses the divine decision turning from mercy to judgment, and cites the story of Rabbi Joshua ben Korha: a father rejoices at a son's birth knowing the child will die, so God made humanity knowing it would sin. Take the quiet reading: this is the sorrow of a maker over what he made. 'To his heart' (el libbo) is inward, like a speech to oneself.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of nacham: be sorry, relent, change one's mind; also related to 'comfort'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban: the Torah speaks in human terms. Rashi: a change from the attribute of mercy to the attribute of judgment.
'Was pained, grieved'. Same root as 'etsev' (pain) in Genesis 3:16-17. Radak compares 2 Samuel 19:3, 'the king was grieved for his son'.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH said, "I will wipe out the human whom I created from upon the face of the ground, from human unto animal, unto creeping thing, and unto bird of the heavens; for I regret that I made them."
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD said, "I will wipe them away: the man I made, from the face of the ground. Man and beast, the creeping things, even the birds of the sky. I am sorry that I made them."
verses.directors_commentary: The decision is spoken in the first person, and it is the first time God speaks of a plan of this size. 'Emcheh' (I will wipe) is the verb for wiping a dish or erasing writing; it is not 'destroy' as in KJV. The image is a scribe or a housewife with a cloth, and Rashi notices the fit: man is dust, and water wipes dust away. The list runs from the top of the order of creation to the bottom, like the list of Genesis 1: human, animal, creeping thing, bird, the same categories God called good. Un-creation is being announced in the order of creation. 'Bara'ti' (I created) uses the verb reserved for God. And the sorrow of verse 6 returns word for word, 'niḥamti', now framed as the reason, 'for I regret'. Why the animals? Rashi and Radak: all were made for man, and without him what is the point of them (the other rabbinic opinion is that animals too corrupted their kind). Director's note: the speech is to himself or to Noah (Ibn Ezra, Radak leave it open), and should sound resolved but not cold.

philological_notes.note: 'I will wipe out, blot out' (as of writing or a dish). Rashi: dust is wiped by water, hence this verb. KJV 'destroy' loses the image.
'Creeping thing', small crawling creatures; Radak counts them among the small living things.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah found favor in the eyes of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The shortest verse in the passage is the hinge, and the beat before it is silence. 'Chen' (favor, grace) is a gift, not a wage: the verse does not say Noah earned it, and Radak cites Genesis Rabbah (on 'but Noah?!') that even Noah was not strictly deserving but found grace; Sforno says his sons were saved by the same grace. Hebrew 'chen' reversed is 'Noach': the name Noah spelled backwards is 'chen' (grace), the sound play every ancient listener hears, because the consonants are the same. KJV's 'grace' is acceptable; 'found favor' is the sense. 'In the eyes of' marks judgment by sight, the same sense as the repeated 'saw' in this passage. Ramban notes the contrast: the generation's deeds were painful to God, Noah's pleasing.

philological_notes.note: 'Favor, grace'. Noah (נח) spelled backwards gives chen (חן), a wordplay on the name. This is my own observation, not a claim of the commentators in the packet.

verses.translation_literal: These [are] the generations of Noah. Noah [was] a man righteous, blameless he was in his generations; with the God walked Noah.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is the story of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, whole and blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.
verses.directors_commentary: A new section begins with the formula 'these are the generations' (toledot), and the name 'Noah' lands three times in one verse, which Radak calls a literary flourish. The verse piles three descriptions: 'tsaddik' (righteous), 'tamim' (blameless, whole) and 'walked with God'. 'Tsaddik' is a legal word: the one in the right, acquitted (Ramban); 'tamim' is the word for an unblemished sacrificial animal, here moral wholeness. Sforno splits them: righteous in deed, whole in thought. KJV's 'just' and 'perfect' are old; 'perfect' wrongly suggests sinlessness. 'Bedorotav', 'in his generations', is the famous crux: Rashi records two rabbinic readings, praise ('how much more had he lived among the righteous') or faint praise ('righteous only for his generation, nothing beside Abraham'); Ramban reads it plainly: he alone was righteous in all those generations. The plural 'generations' is kept. 'Hithallekh', the reflexive 'walked about with', is a verb of habitual closeness; Rashi observes that Abraham 'walked before' God, Noah 'with' him, and takes this as a lesser independence. Also note Noah is called 'ish' a man, with the full dignity of the word.

philological_notes.note: 'Righteous, blameless'. Ramban: tsaddik is the legal sense, in the right; Ibn Ezra: righteous in deeds, whole in heart; Sforno: righteous in action, whole in knowledge. Tamim also describes an unblemished offering.
'In his generations', plural. Rashi records praise and faint-praise readings; Ramban: he was the only one righteous in all those generations.
Hithpael, 'walked about, walked habitually'. Rashi contrasts Noah 'with God' and Abraham 'before God'.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah fathered three sons: [obj] Shem, [obj] Ham, and [obj] Japheth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verses.directors_commentary: A plain roll call, delivered evenly, as a clerk would read names, and the repeated marker 'et' before each name makes the list sound like a ledger. Genesis 5:32 already told us this; the repetition is purposeful. Radak: it is repeated after 'Noah walked with God' to show that Noah taught his sons the same way, which is why they were saved; Ramban: the point is that Noah, unlike his forefathers, had no further sons or daughters, only these three who would survive. The order is by prominence, not birth: Ramban argues Japheth was the eldest and Ham the youngest. KJV says 'begat', a standard archaism; modern readers should hear 'fathered'. In a world where inheritance and survival went through sons, three sons meant a family line secure enough to carry a new world.

verses.translation_literal: And the earth was corrupt before the God, and the earth was filled [with] violence.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the earth rotted in the sight of God. The earth was filled with violence.
verses.directors_commentary:
The noun repeats: the earth... the earth, like a drumbeat. Ibn Ezra and Radak say 'the earth' stands for the people on it. 'Vatishachet' (was corrupted, spoiled, ruined) is the root shachat, and it returns twice in verse 12 (nishchatah, hishchit) and again in verse 13 (mashchitam, 'I will destroy them'): the word that names the crime is the word that names the sentence, so the earth is given what it did. KJV's 'also' (the earth also was corrupt) adds a link the Hebrew does not have.

The key noun is 'chamas', violence: not a vague wickedness but wrongful seizure by force, robbery, oppression (Rashi: robbery; Ibn Ezra: theft, extortion, and taking women by force). It is the wrong that left the weak with no recourse, and it echoes what verse 2 hinted at in the taking. 'Before the God' puts the wrong in front of the judge; Ibn Ezra says the Torah speaks like a servant who does wrong in front of his master and does not fear him. Rashi hears in the verb sexual immorality and idolatry (citing Deuteronomy 4:16).

philological_notes.note: Niphal of shachat: be corrupted, ruined, spoiled. Rashi hears sexual immorality and idolatry in it (citing Deut 4:16). The same root returns in verse 12 (nishchatah, hishchit) and verse 13 (mashchitam).
Violence, wrongful force, robbery. Rashi: robbery; Ibn Ezra: theft, extortion and seizing women by force.

verses.translation_literal: And God saw the earth, and behold, it [was] corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God looked upon the earth, and there it lay, ruined. For all flesh had spoiled its own way on the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb 'saw' comes round again. After creation, God saw and it was good; now God sees and 'hinneh': behold, it is corrupt. The word 'hinneh' gives the audience the shock of seeing with God. Hear the echo: 'nishchatah' (it was corrupt), 'hishchit' (had corrupted): the earth is ruined because flesh ruined its way. 'Its way' is 'darko': Radak reads it as the way of its nature or kind, how each creature was made to go; Ibn Ezra and Rashi hear animals as well, Ramban prefers humankind only, and 'kol basar' (all flesh) elsewhere means every living body. KJV's 'his way' is a faithful singular (the Hebrew is a collective singular), where ASV changes to 'their'. 'All flesh' picks up 'he is flesh' from verse 3. Sforno's point is chilling: the earth was already on its way to ruin by itself, without any punishment. Play the beat before the next verse, God's announcement to Noah, in stillness.

philological_notes.note: 'All flesh'. Ramban: here, humankind; Rashi: even beasts and birds in their mating; Radak: human beings, though the rabbis include the animals.
'Its way': a creature's proper course or nature (Radak: the way of its begetting). Ibn Ezra: each living thing did not keep its natural path.

verses.translation_literal: And God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is full of violence from before them, and here I [am] ruining them, [together with] the earth."
verses.translation_dramatic: And God spoke to Noah, and the words came slowly, one weight laid upon another. "The end of all flesh has come before me. The earth is filled with violence, brimming over, and it is all because of them. See: I am the one who will ruin them, and the earth beneath them."
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a verdict delivered to a friend, not a tantrum. God has just looked at the earth and found it ruined (6:12); now the sentence is read to the one man who will be spared. Note the sound play the KJV cannot carry: the verb for 'ruin' (shachat) is the same root that described the earth's own state in 6:11-12. The earth is ruined by what its creatures did, and so God will ruin them. The punishment is built from the crime's own vocabulary.

The KJV's 'is filled with violence through them' is serviceable but soft. The Hebrew says the earth is full of chamas 'from before them' - their faces, their presence, are the source. Chamas is not a general word for sin: it means violent wrong, robbery and oppression of the weak, and the rabbis (Rashi, Ramban, Radak, all citing Sanhedrin 108) note that the decree was sealed on this and not on idolatry or sexual wrongdoing. Sforno spells out its everyday shape: owners robbing tenants by force, tenants robbing owners by fraud. For an ancient audience living on the margin, where land and its produce were everything, a land that gave its harvest only to the strong was a land that had stopped working.

The last words are a puzzle. 'et ha'aretz' after 'ruining them' can mean 'with the earth' (the KJV), or 'from the earth' (Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra all cite 'et' used for 'min' elsewhere), or the earth itself is a second object of the ruin. The actors should not choose too cleanly: the earth shares the sentence.

philological_notes.note: Violence in the sense of wrongful, brutal seizure: robbery, oppression, bloodshed. The rabbinic tradition treats it as the one sin that sealed the generation's fate.
'Ruining them'. The same root as in 6:11-12 (the earth was ruined), so the sentence mirrors the offence.
Ambiguous: 'with the earth', 'from the earth', or the earth as a second object.

verses.translation_literal: Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood; nests you shall make [in] the ark, and you shall cover it, from inside and from outside, with the cover.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Make yourself an ark, Noah, of gopher wood. Build it as a hive of small rooms, nest beside nest. Then seal it, inside and out, with pitch, so that no water finds a way in."
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a work order, spoken in short imperatives, and Noah says nothing. Many English readers hear 'ark' as a boat, but the Hebrew tevah is not a ship's word. It occurs only here and for the basket of baby Moses in Exodus; Ibn Ezra notes it is called a tevah rather than a ship because it has no oars and no ship's shape. It is a floating box built to survive, not to travel.

The KJV gives 'rooms'; the Hebrew is qinnim, literally 'nests', the word used for birds' nests. The image is of many small compartments, one for each pair, which Rashi and Radak take as separate dwellings for each kind. 'Gopher' is not a tree anyone can identify: it occurs once in the Bible. Onkelos translates it kadrom and Radak calls it a light wood of the cedar family, but that is a tradition, not a certainty.

The KJV's 'pitch it ... with pitch' hides a wordplay: the verb vekhafarta and the noun kofer are the same root, so the Hebrew says 'cover it with the covering'. This root later becomes the Hebrew word for atonement (kapper, 'to cover' sin). No ancient reader would miss that the thing that saves Noah from the flood is called a kofer. The bitumen itself was familiar to a Mesopotamian audience, where reed boats were routinely sealed with it. Radak reads 'inside and outside' as insurance: if the outer coat fails under the force of the water, the inner one holds.

philological_notes.note: 'Ark'. Used only here (the flood) and for the basket of Moses (Exodus 2). A vessel for rescue, not a ship; Ibn Ezra stresses it has no oars.
A word found only here. Onkelos has kadrom; Radak says a light wood of the cedar kind. Its identity is lost.
'Nests'. The ordinary word for a bird's nest, applied here to compartments in the ark.
A verb and noun of the same root: 'cover with the covering', i.e. pitch. The same root gives the later Hebrew word for atonement.

verses.translation_literal: And this [is that] which you shall make it: three hundred cubit[s], the length of the ark; fifty cubit[s], its breadth; and thirty cubit[s], its height.
verses.translation_dramatic: And these are the measures by which you will build it. Three hundred cubits from end to end, the length of the ark. Fifty cubits across, its breadth. And thirty cubits high, its towering height.
verses.directors_commentary:
God turns from material to measure, and the speech goes flat on purpose: no adjectives, only numbers. Three hundred, fifty, thirty. Let the actor read them like a surveyor reading a plan, because that is the register of the text. The numbers carry their own awe. In ordinary terms a cubit is about 45 cm (roughly the forearm from elbow to fingertip), so the vessel is about 135 m long, 22.5 m wide and 13.5 m high, the height of a four-storey building and a hull longer than a football pitch. No ancient family could have thought of building such a thing; that is the point of being told the figures.

The proportions are the quiet genius of the verse: the breadth is one sixth of the length and the height one tenth, a ratio of 30:5:3. Ibn Ezra and Radak both read this as engineering: so shaped, the ark rides level on the water and is not overturned by wind or wave, and Radak adds that Genesis Rabbah took it as the Torah teaching worldly practice, that a ship's width should be a sixth of its length and its height a tenth. Note too that this is a box, not a boat: no keel, no prow, no sail, no rudder is mentioned. It floats; it does not sail. It goes where the water takes it, which suits a story in which Noah steers nothing and God shuts the door.

The KJV's 'this is the fashion which thou shalt make it of' is archaic and clumsy. 'Fashion' obscures that zeh is simply 'this', the measure itself, and the Hebrew has no 'of'. The KJV also fills in 'shall be' and 'is', which the Hebrew leaves bare; the verse is three verbless clauses, three numbers set down like entries in a ledger. The Hebrew also places each number first, before the dimension it measures, so the numbers arrive before the things. The word 'cubit' follows every figure, three times, like a drumbeat; keep it in the delivery.

philological_notes.note: The cubit, the forearm measure from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, about 45 cm in common use. The word is repeated after every figure, which gives the verse its ledger rhythm.
'Its height', literally its 'standing up', from the root 'to rise, to stand'. The same root names a thing's stature, so the ark is measured by how tall it stands.

'Length', from the root 'to be long'. Ibn Ezra reads the whole verse as a statement of proportion, the height one tenth of the length, so that the ark floats on the surface and the wind does not overturn it.

verses.translation_literal: A tzohar you shall make for the ark, and to a cubit you shall finish it from above; and the entrance of the ark in its side you shall put; lower, second and third [decks] you shall make it.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Give the ark a tzohar, a place for light, and finish it a cubit from the top. Set the door in its side. And make it three decks, the lower, the second and the third."
verses.directors_commentary:
More specifications, but now the interior begins to appear: a source of light, a door, three floors. Let the actor feel the darkness these instructions imply, a sealed box with one opening high in the roof and one door that will be shut behind the family.

The key word is tzohar. The KJV and the others say 'window' (the later account uses a different word, challon, in 8:6). But tzohar occurs only here, and it is related to tzohorayim, 'noon': it is a 'noonlight', an opening for daylight. Rashi and Radak preserve an old rabbinic alternative, a shining gem that lit the ark. We keep the word untranslated in the literal layer because we cannot know whether it was a window, a skylight, a gap beneath the eaves, or a stone.

The clause 'to a cubit you shall finish it from above' is equally obscure. The KJV reads 'in a cubit shalt thou finish it above', and Rashi and Radak picture a sloping roof that narrows until a single cubit remains at the top, so that rain runs off. Ibn Ezra reads the same line as a tapering form that cannot tip over. The three decks (tachtiyim, shenim, shelishim) are 'lower, second, third', and the old rabbis argued over which floor held humans, animals and refuse. Ibn Ezra notes even the odd spelling of the words, and Sforno compares the layout to the decks familiar to sailors.

philological_notes.note: Found only here. Connected to the noun for noon (tzohorayim): an opening for light. Possibly a window or skylight; some rabbinic readings take it as a radiant gem.
'Lower, second and third [decks]'. The plural adjectives stand alone, so the noun (decks, stories) must be supplied.

verses.translation_literal: And I, here I [am] bringing the flood, water, upon the earth, to ruin all flesh in which [is] the breath of life from under the heavens; everything that [is] on the earth shall expire.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And I, I myself, am about to bring the flood: water over all the earth, to ruin every creature that has the breath of life in it, everywhere under heaven. Everything that is on the earth will breathe its last."
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone shifts from carpenter's briefing to cosmic threat, and the word 'I' is doubled for weight: va'ani hineni, 'and I, behold me'. Ramban hears in that emphasis that God Himself will take a hand in the destruction. The speaker is not announcing a natural disaster; he is claiming it.

The KJV 'a flood of waters' smooths over an odd Hebrew phrase: 'the mabbul, water'. Mabbul is a rare word used almost only of this event (and once in Psalm 29), so the text spells out what it means with the plain word 'water', just as an explanatory gloss. Radak connects it with a root meaning 'to fall' and so rain pouring from the sky, and Rashi plays on 'to confuse' and 'to carry down'.

The verb 'to ruin' is again shachat, the same root as in 6:11-13. The phrase 'breath of life' (ruach chayyim) points back to Genesis 2:7: what God breathed in, He will let go out. The final word, yigva', 'shall expire', is the language of the last gasp, not a neutral 'die'. Radak limits the decree to land creatures, since fish are not among those who share the earth with humans.

philological_notes.note: 'The flood'. A rare word, tied to the flood alone. Medieval commentators derive it from a root meaning 'to fall' or 'to mix'.
'Breath of life', the breath given at creation in Genesis 2:7.
'To expire'. A poetic verb for dying, literally giving up the breath.

verses.translation_literal: And I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you and your sons and your wife and the wives of your sons with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: "But with you, Noah, I will set up my covenant. And you will walk into the ark, you and your sons, and your wife, and your sons' wives with you."
verses.directors_commentary:
One quiet sentence in the middle of the thunder. After judgment on 'all flesh', God turns to one man and says 'my covenant', the first appearance of the word berit in the Bible. Play the beat as relief, but a heavy relief: Noah is told that he will live, and told in the same breath how many will not.

The KJV's opening 'But' is not in the Hebrew; the verse begins 'and', and the contrast is in the sense, not the grammar. The verb is hakim, 'to establish', 'to set up', not the usual 'to cut' (karat) a covenant: it speaks of a promise already standing and now to be confirmed. Ibn Ezra reads it as a divine oath that Noah and his sons will not die in the flood, and links the covenant to the rainbow later; Ramban and Radak read it as the pledge of rescue.

Note the sequence of the family: Noah, sons, wife, sons' wives. The men and the women are named in separate groups, which the rabbis (Rashi, Radak, citing Genesis Rabbah) took as a sign that couples were kept apart during the year of the flood. That is interpretation, not what the text says.

philological_notes.note: 'My covenant'. The first covenant in the Bible. With the verb 'establish' (hakim) it describes the confirming of an existing commitment.
'And I will establish', literally 'cause to stand'.

verses.translation_literal: And of every living [thing], of all flesh, two of everything you shall bring into the ark, to keep alive with you; male and female they shall be.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And from every living creature, from all flesh, two of each you shall bring into the ark, to keep them alive with you. A male and a female, each pair."
verses.directors_commentary:
The scope widens from one family to the whole living world, and the language is the language of a roll call. Every phrase here repeats 'of all, of every, of everything': the Hebrew piles up the totals.

The verb is the key. Lehachayot means 'to keep alive', 'to give life to': Noah is not a zookeeper but a lifesaver, and the verb is the same one used for what God does. The KJV's 'to keep them alive' is fine, but 'with you' is crucial: the animals are in the ark with Noah, in the same breath, and not merely under him.

The fine point is 'zachar unqevah', 'male and female', the very wording of Genesis 1:27 for humankind. The animals are, like humans, created for continuing generations. Ramban argues that the size of the ark could never hold all species with a year's food and calls the matter a miracle; Radak says God would stir the animals to come on their own. Rashi's remark that even demons were included is a rabbinic aside the text does not support.

philological_notes.note: 'To keep alive'. A causative verb: Noah is the agent of preserving life.
'Male and female'. The same pair of words as in Genesis 1:27.

verses.translation_literal: Of the birds according to their kind, and of the animals according to their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground according to its kind, two of everything shall come to you, to keep alive.
verses.translation_dramatic: "The birds, each after its own kind. The beasts, each after its own kind. Everything that creeps on the ground, each after its own kind. Two of each will come to you, and you will keep them alive."
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a litany; read it as a list that the voice of God walks through slowly, bird, beast, creeping thing, the same three orders as in the creation account of Genesis 1.

The small but crucial verb is yavo'u, 'they shall come': the animals come to Noah. He is not told to hunt them. Ibn Ezra, Ramban and Radak all stress that the animals come of themselves, and Radak imagines God stirring their instincts. The KJV 'shall come unto thee' keeps it, but the BBE ('will you take') loses it. The detail matters for staging: Noah stands at the door, and the creatures arrive.

The refrain lemino, 'after its kind', is the language of Genesis 1, here marking each species as a distinct line to be preserved. The commentators (Ibn Ezra, Ramban) note that this verse speaks of a pair of each, and that the later instruction in 7:2 for seven pairs of clean animals is added afterwards, for sacrifice. Do not harmonise the two in performance: here, the pair is the whole instruction.

philological_notes.note: 'According to its kind'. The classification word of Genesis 1.
'They shall come': the animals arrive of their own accord.

verses.translation_literal: And you, take for yourself of every food that is eaten, and you shall gather [it] to yourself, and it shall be for you and for them for food.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And you, Noah, take for yourself some of every kind of food that can be eaten. Gather it in, store it close. It will be food for you, and food for them."
verses.directors_commentary:
The practical heart of the whole plan. Salvation is not only a boat; it is a larder. The verse begins with a stressed 'and you' (ve'attah), turning the focus back to Noah after the animals' list: this part is yours.

The KJV 'take thou unto thee' captures the double 'to yourself', and the Hebrew is blunt about it: 'take for yourself ... gather to yourself'. The actor can lean on the repeated possessive. The same Hebrew root ('akhal, eat) appears three times in the verse: the food that 'is eaten' becomes 'food'. Radak says that the food in question is fruit, seed and grass, and that even predators were then fed on it, as at the creation (Genesis 1:29-30). That is his reading of an unstated detail; the text only says 'every food that is eaten'.

An ancient audience knew the arithmetic of a year's provisions for a household and animals, a thing no farmer took lightly. The sentence is a quiet reminder of how enormous the task is.

philological_notes.note: 'Food'. With 'it is eaten' and 'for food' (le'okhlah), the root appears three times in one verse.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah did according to all that God commanded him; so he did.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Noah did it. All of it, exactly as God had commanded him. So he did.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter closes without a word from Noah, who has not spoken once. The action is the answer. Play the silence: after the longest speech of God yet in the Bible, the response is two short verbs.

The KJV 'Thus did Noah' is accurate in sense but the Hebrew has a doubled structure: 'Noah did ... so he did' (vayya'as ... ken asah). Ramban explains the repetition as a way of saying that he left nothing out. Rashi reads the verse as a reference to the building of the ark; Radak extends it to the measurements, the compartments and the food.

The verse echoes the end of the creation story and the later completion of the Tabernacle, where 'as God commanded' marks a work faithfully done. For an ancient audience the contrast is with the preceding generation, who did what they wished and filled the earth with violence.

philological_notes.note: 'So he did'. The repetition of 'did' closes the verse and shows nothing was left out.

events.title: The sons of God take the daughters of men as wives
events.narrative_summary: As humankind multiplies and daughters are born, the sons of God see that the daughters of men are fair and take wives from whomever they choose.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives only 'when mankind began to multiply' (6:1), no number. Placed about 1450 years after anchor.creation, before the decree of 6:3 (at 1535 y), margin 300 years for the lack of any date; MACRO_ERA. Duration of 50 years for the taking of wives is an estimate for a process, not an act.
events.ancient_year_marker: When mankind began to multiply on the face of the ground

events.title: The LORD limits humankind to 120 years
events.narrative_summary: The LORD says his spirit will not remain in humankind for ever, since they are flesh, and sets their days at one hundred and twenty years.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Counted back from the Flood: Noah was 600 at the Flood (7:6; anchor.flood = creation + 1655 y), so 120 years earlier is creation + 1535 y (Noah 480). This reads the 120 years as a term before the Flood (Onkelos, Ps-Jonathan, Sforno citing Sanh. 108b), not as a new human lifespan. The speech itself takes minutes; margin 5 years because the Flood date is exact only by the Masoretic count. MACRO_ERA: the text gives a term, not a dated moment.

events.title: The Nephilim and the heroes of old arise
events.narrative_summary: The Nephilim are on the earth in those days and afterwards, when the sons of God go in to the daughters of men and they bear children, who are the mighty men of old, men of renown.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 6:4 'in those days, and also after that' describes a span after the marriages of 6:1–2. Anchored on their END with a 20-year delay for the first children to be born and a 40-year span; margin 60 years because the text gives no number. Rashi and Ramban date it to the generation of Enosh, before the Flood. MACRO_ERA.
events.ancient_year_marker: In those days, and also afterward

events.title: The LORD sees human evil and regrets making humankind
events.narrative_summary: The LORD sees that human evil is great and every inclination of their hearts only evil, regrets and grieves that he made them, and resolves to wipe them out; Noah finds favour in his eyes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 6:5–8 follow the decree of 6:3 without an interval and express the same judgement, so the event starts with it (offset 0, START) and lasts a day for an inner act of seeing and speaking. Margin 5 years, as the decree. 'All the day' (6:5) describes human continual evil, not the time of the divine reaction. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Noah, a righteous man, fathers Shem, Ham and Japheth
events.narrative_summary: Noah, righteous and blameless in his generation, who walked with God, fathers three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 6:10 gives no age; Gen 5:32 says Noah was 500 when he began to father the three. On the Masoretic chain Noah was born AM 1056, so the births fall at creation + 1555 y. Duration 2 years covers the three births (Shem, according to 11:10, was born at Noah 502); margin 3 years. REGNAL_YEAR because the age frames the birth.
events.ancient_year_marker: When Noah was five hundred years old (Gen 5:32)

events.title: God sees the earth corrupt and full of violence
events.narrative_summary: The earth is corrupt before God and full of violence; God sees that all flesh has corrupted its way on the earth.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A state, undated in the text. Placed 10 years after the sons' birth (END of evt.gen_6.noah_sons_born), because the command that follows speaks of Noah's sons and their wives (6:18), and lasting ten years until the command. Margin 10 years; MACRO_ERA.

events.title: God tells Noah to build an ark and enter it with his family and the animals
events.narrative_summary: God tells Noah that the end of all flesh has come, orders him to build a pitched three-storey ark of gopher wood, announces the flood, promises a covenant, and tells him to bring his family and two of every kind of living thing aboard with food.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 6:13–21 are one continuous speech introduced by a single 'and God said': a command (6:14–16, 19–21) with its announcement (6:13, 17) and promise (6:18). It starts the moment the corrupt state of 6:11–12 ends, and takes about half an hour. Absolute position is about Noah 520, estimated from the presence of sons' wives (6:18) and the 100 years left before the Flood at Noah 600; margin 15 years; MACRO_ERA. Sforno on 6:13 reads 'the end' as the 120 years allotted.

events.title: Noah does all that God commanded
events.narrative_summary: Noah does according to all that God commanded him: so he does.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 6:22 summarizes the execution of the command, which the text does not date. It starts at the END of the command, and lasts 73 years, an estimate that ends at creation + 1650 y, five years before the Flood (creation + 1655 y), leaving that time for Noah's entry into the ark in Gen 7. Margin 5 years. The tradition (Sforno, Sanh. 108b) of 120 years of building would put the command before the sons' birth and does not fit 6:18, so it is not adopted. MACRO_ERA.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Because the earth is full of violence and all flesh has corrupted its way, God announces the end of all flesh and instructs Noah to build the ark (6:11–13).
Noah carries out what God commanded him, and does so in full (6:22, 'according to all that God commanded him').
The LORD's regret and resolve to wipe out humankind (6:6–7) lead him to warn Noah, who found favour, and to prepare his rescue (6:13–14).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew tēbâ, 'chest, box'; used elsewhere only for the basket of baby Moses.
entities.summary_bio: A vessel of gopher wood God tells Noah to build, 300 by 50 by 30 cubits with a roof, a door and three decks, sealed with pitch. It will preserve Noah's family and pairs of every living creature through the flood.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'daughters of the human race', set against the 'sons of God'.
entities.summary_bio: The daughters born as humankind multiplies. The sons of God find them beautiful and take wives from among them.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew gibbôr, 'mighty one, warrior'; 'men of the name' means men of renown.
entities.summary_bio: The mighty men 'of old, men of renown', linked in 6:4 to the union of the sons of God with the daughters of men.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'fallen ones' (from nāpal, 'to fall'); the Septuagint and KJV render 'giants'.
entities.summary_bio: A race on the earth 'in those days, and also afterward'. Genesis 6:4 mentions them beside the heroes of old without saying how they came to be.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'sons of the God/gods', a title for divine or heavenly beings elsewhere (Job 1:6); its meaning here is disputed.
entities.summary_bio: Beings who see that the daughters of men are fair and take wives of their choice. Whether they are heavenly beings, godly men of Seth's line or rulers is debated, and the text does not say.

entities.etymology_meaning: Unnamed in the text; the Hebrew reads 'wives of your sons'.
entities.summary_bio: The three women married to Shem, Ham and Japheth, who are to enter the ark with Noah.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; perhaps 'hot' or 'warm', or connected to an Egyptian word.
entities.summary_bio: Second-listed son of Noah, who enters the ark with his father, brothers and their wives.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'may he enlarge' (from pātâ / pātâ), as in a wordplay of Genesis 9:27.
entities.summary_bio: Third-listed son of Noah, who enters the ark with his father, brothers and their wives.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'rest' or 'comfort' (from nûaḥ / nāḥam); Genesis 5:29 links the name to 'comfort'.
entities.summary_bio: A righteous and blameless man who walks with God, and who finds favour with the LORD when all else is corrupt. He fathers Shem, Ham and Japheth, and builds the ark as God commands.

entities.etymology_meaning: Unnamed in the text; the Hebrew simply reads 'your wife'.
entities.summary_bio: The wife of Noah, mentioned among those God tells Noah to bring into the ark.
Eldest-listed son of Noah, named first of his three sons. He is among those God tells Noah to bring into the ark.

components.evidence_explanation: GEN.6.3: "his days shall be an hundred and twenty years." The verse is read either as a limit on the human lifespan or, with Onkelos, as a 120-year term of respite before the Flood; the label follows the words of the verse and does not choose.
Gen 6:5: every inclination of the thoughts of the heart was only evil all day.
Gen 6:9: Noah was a righteous, blameless man in his generations.
Gen 6:8: Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD.
Gen 6:6: the LORD regretted making humankind and was pained at heart.

systems.name: Promise of a covenant
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Covenants joined parties by oath and obligation; in Genesis God binds himself by promise to a chosen person.
rules_and_mechanics: A named person and household are the covenant's recipients.
The covenant is announced first and established later.

systems.name: Divine command to an individual
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the ancient Near East the gods addressed kings and chosen persons through dreams, oracles and intermediaries, often with detailed building instructions (as for temples). Genesis gives God's speech directly and in unusual detail.
rules_and_mechanics: God speaks to a chosen individual.
The command carries exact specifications and a purpose.
The right response is full, literal obedience.

systems.name: Divine decree
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A god's pronouncement set a limit or a fate for people, as in Mesopotamian myths where the gods decree the length of human life.
rules_and_mechanics: The LORD speaks a sentence on humankind.
The decree fixes a limit or a consequence.
It is spoken in response to the people's condition.

systems.name: Divine judgment by flood
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Flood stories are known in Mesopotamian texts (Atrahasis, Gilgamesh), where gods send a flood to destroy humanity; here the cause is violence and corruption, and one family is preserved.
rules_and_mechanics: The judgment answers the earth's corruption and violence.
All flesh with the breath of life is to die.
One righteous person and his household are spared.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God gives Noah exact instructions for the ark, the animals to bring in and food to store.
system_instances.significance_note: Makes Noah the means of preserving life through the flood.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God promises to establish his covenant with Noah and tells him to enter the ark with his family.
system_instances.significance_note: First use of the covenant promise in the Bible; it is fulfilled in Genesis 9.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God tells Noah that the end of all flesh has come and that he will bring a flood to destroy it.
system_instances.significance_note: Tells Noah why the ark is needed.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD resolves to wipe humankind, with animals and birds, from the ground.
system_instances.significance_note: Opens the judgment that the flood will carry out.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD says his spirit will not remain in humankind for ever and limits their days to 120 years.
system_instances.significance_note: Sets a limit before the flood narrative begins.

edges.description: God commands Noah to make an ark of gopher wood.
God says he will establish his covenant with Noah.
Noah does all that God commanded him.
The sons of God have children with the daughters of men, apparently the mighty men of old.
The sons of God take wives from all the daughters of men whom they chose.
Noah finds favour in the eyes of the LORD.
The LORD limits humankind's days to 120 years.
The LORD resolves to wipe out humankind and the animals from the ground.
